learningObjective: Identify true statements about TorchInductor's CPU C++ backend and how it differs from the CUDA Triton backend.

canonicalClaims.claim: TorchInductor targets a CPU backend that generates C++ code with OpenMP parallel loops and CPU vector intrinsics, compiled via a system compiler; the graph-level IR and Inductor lowerings are shared with the CUDA Triton backend, which diverges at codegen. Backend selection follows the device of the input tensors.
conditions: The user has not forced a backend override.
nonImplications: Does not imply the C++ backend beats vendor CPU libraries (oneDNN, MKL) on every op.
Does not imply identical op coverage between CPU and CUDA backends.

misconceptions.claim: Inductor offloads reductions from CPU to CUDA transparently.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Device dispatch is respected; Inductor does not silently cross devices.

misconceptions.claim: The CPU backend uses Triton to generate code.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Triton targets NVIDIA (and now AMD) GPUs; the CPU backend emits C++.
Backend follows the input tensor device by default.

misconceptions.claim: CPU and CUDA backends have entirely separate IRs and lowerings.
misconceptions.whyWrong: They share Inductor's graph-level IR and lowerings; codegen is where they diverge.

implementationFacts: C++ backend uses OpenMP for parallel loops
Vector intrinsics: AVX2 / AVX-512 / NEON depending on target
System compiler (typically g++/clang) builds a shared library that Python loads
performanceScenarios: Compiled CPU code can outperform eager op-dispatch overhead on many small ops; vendor libraries still win on some kernels.
